subject: Medicine
summary: Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC) is an acquired syndrome of simultaneous widespread clotting and bleeding caused by uncontrolled activation of coagulation throughout the microvasculature.

sections.p: DIC is a systemic consumptive coagulopathy where clotting factors and platelets are used up faster than they can be replaced, leading to both thrombosis and bleeding.
b: Diagnosed by a combination of clinical bleeding, organ dysfunction, and laboratory evidence of consumption coagulopathy.

t.b: Is there thrombocytopenia? Low platelets support DIC and indicate severity.
Are clotting times prolonged? Prolongation reflects factor consumption.
Is fibrinogen low (<1.0 g/L)? Low fibrinogen is a key consumptive marker.
Are they markedly elevated? High levels show ongoing fibrinolysis.
Are schistocytes present? They indicate microvascular thrombi.

sections.p: The ISTH scoring system grades DIC from overt to non‑overt based on platelet count, fibrinogen, PT prolongation, and D‑dimer.
b: Score ≥5 = overt DIC (requires treatment).
Score <5 = non‑overt (monitor and treat underlying cause).

sections.p: Identify the trigger; treatment hinges on removing it.
b: Sepsis (especially Gram‑negative) – most common worldwide.
Obstetric emergencies: abruptio placentae, amniotic fluid embolism, severe pre‑eclampsia/eclampsia.
Acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL) – high‑risk malignancy.
Severe trauma or massive transfusion.
Incompatible blood transfusion reactions.

sections.p: Patients may show bleeding from venipuncture sites, mucous membranes, or surgical wounds, alongside signs of organ ischemia such as renal failure or altered mental status.
b: Bleeding: petechiae, ecchymoses, oozing drains.
Thrombosis: skin necrosis, digital gangrene, pulmonary emboli.
Systemic: hypotension, oliguria, confusion.

sections.p: Lab work confirms consumptive coagulopathy; imaging is guided by organ dysfunction.
b: Basic coagulation panel (platelets, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, D‑dimer).
Blood smear for schistocytes.
Renal and liver function tests to gauge organ injury.

t.b: Is there organ infarction? Detects renal or hepatic ischemia when labs suggest dysfunction.
Is there pulmonary infiltrate? Helps differentiate sepsis‑related ARDS from pulmonary emboli.

sections.p: Rapid progression can cause fatal hemorrhage or multi‑organ failure.
b: Uncontrolled bleeding despite transfusion.
Sudden rise in creatinine or liver enzymes.
Severe hypotension unresponsive to fluids.

sections.p: Treat the underlying trigger first, then support the coagulation system while avoiding over‑correction.
b: Treat cause: antibiotics for sepsis, delivery of fetus for obstetric DIC, ATRA for APL.
Replace depleted components: Fresh frozen plasma (provides clotting factors), cryoprecipitate (fibrinogen), platelet concentrates (if <50 × 10⁹/L or bleeding).
Consider low‑dose heparin only in chronic, low‑bleeding DIC with predominant thrombosis.

sections.p: Monitor labs every 6–12 h until stable; educate on early infection control and obstetric care to reduce triggers.
b: Serial platelet, PT/INR, fibrinogen, D‑dimer.
Re‑evaluate cause treatment effectiveness.
Vaccination and prophylactic antibiotics in high‑risk patients.

sections.p: Conditions that also cause bleeding or thrombosis but have different mechanisms.
b: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) – ADAMTS13 deficiency, mainly neurologic signs.
Severe liver disease – reduced synthesis without consumptive clotting.
Heparin‑induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) – immune platelet activation, not consumptive.

sections.p: Certain labs may appear normal early or be altered by other factors.
b: Fibrinogen can be falsely normal in acute phase reactant rise despite consumption.
D‑dimer may be elevated in infection alone, not specific for DIC.
PT may stay within range early; trend over time is more informative.

faq.q: Why does DIC cause both clotting and bleeding?
faq.a: Widespread clot formation uses up platelets and factors, leaving insufficient resources for normal hemostasis, so bleeding follows.
Prompt treatment of common triggers (sepsis, obstetric complications) and early infection control reduce risk.

faq.q: When is heparin appropriate in DIC?
faq.a: Only in chronic, low‑bleeding DIC where thrombosis dominates and platelet/fibrinogen levels are adequate.

exam: Explain the pathophysiology of DIC and why it leads to simultaneous thrombosis and hemorrhage.
List the ISTH criteria for overt DIC and interpret a sample laboratory set.
Describe the first‑line management steps for a septic patient who develops DIC.
